title: Electricity & Magnetism II
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 200L Electricity and Magnetism II curriculum, building on PHY201: magnetostatics (Biot-Savart law, Ampere's law, force on moving charges and current-carrying conductors, torque on a current loop), electromagnetic induction (Faraday's and Lenz's laws, self- and mutual inductance, motional EMF), AC circuit theory (RMS values, reactance, impedance, series RLC resonance, power factor), and introductory magnetic properties of materials. Electrostatics and DC circuit theory are deliberately excluded, as they belong to PHY201.

questions.question: The Biot-Savart law is used to calculate:
options: The magnetic field produced at a point by a small current-carrying element
The electric field produced by a point charge
The force between two point charges
The capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor
questions.correct_answer: The magnetic field produced at a point by a small current-carrying element
questions.explanation: The Biot-Savart law gives the contribution dB to the magnetic field at a point due to a small current element Idl, which can then be integrated over the full conductor.

questions.question: According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnitude of the magnetic field dB due to a current element is:
options: Proportional to the current and the sine of the angle between the element and the position vector, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance
Proportional to the square of the distance from the element
Independent of the current in the element
Proportional only to the length of the element, regardless of distance
questions.correct_answer: Proportional to the current and the sine of the angle between the element and the position vector, and inversely proportional to the square of the distance
questions.explanation: dB = (mu0/4pi) x I dl sin(theta) / r^2, so it depends on current, the sine of the angle between dl and the line to the field point, and falls off as 1/r^2.

questions.question: Using the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field at the centre of a circular current loop of radius R carrying current I is given by:
questions.correct_answer: B = mu0 I / (2R)
questions.explanation: Integrating the Biot-Savart law around a full circular loop, with every element perpendicular to the radius, gives B = mu0 I/(2R) at the centre.

questions.question: The magnetic field at a perpendicular distance r from a long, straight current-carrying conductor is given by:
questions.correct_answer: B = mu0 I / (2 pi r)
questions.explanation: This is the standard result obtained from Ampere's law (or the Biot-Savart law) for an infinite straight wire: the field circles the wire and falls off as 1/r.

questions.question: Ampere's circuital law relates the line integral of the magnetic field around a closed loop to:
options: The total current enclosed by that loop, multiplied by the permeability of free space
The total charge enclosed by the loop
The rate of change of electric flux through the loop only
questions.correct_answer: The total current enclosed by that loop, multiplied by the permeability of free space
questions.explanation: Ampere's law states that the closed line integral of B.dl around any loop equals mu0 times the net current passing through the loop.

questions.question: Ampere's law is most conveniently applied to find the magnetic field in situations with:
options: High symmetry, such as a long straight wire, a solenoid, or a toroid
Only isolated point charges at rest
Static electric fields with no current present
questions.correct_answer: High symmetry, such as a long straight wire, a solenoid, or a toroid
questions.explanation: Like Gauss's law in electrostatics, Ampere's law is only easy to solve for B directly when a symmetric Amperian loop can be chosen along which B is constant in magnitude.

questions.question: Using Ampere's law, the magnetic field inside a long solenoid with n turns per unit length carrying current I is given by:
questions.correct_answer: B = mu0 n I
questions.explanation: Applying Ampere's law to a rectangular loop partly inside and partly outside a long, tightly wound solenoid gives the uniform interior field B = mu0 n I.

questions.question: The magnetic force on a charged particle of charge q moving with velocity v in a magnetic field B is given by:
options: F = qv x B (the vector cross product)
questions.correct_answer: F = qv x B (the vector cross product)
questions.explanation: The magnetic (Lorentz) force is F = qv x B, meaning its magnitude depends on the sine of the angle between v and B and its direction is perpendicular to both.

questions.question: A charged particle moving with velocity v parallel to a magnetic field B (i.e., along the field direction) experiences:
options: A force perpendicular to both v and B
A force that increases the particle's speed
questions.correct_answer: Zero magnetic force
questions.explanation: Since F = qvB sin(theta), when v is parallel to B, theta = 0 and sin(theta) = 0, giving zero force.

questions.question: A charged particle moving perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field travels in a path that is:
options: A circle, because the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity
A straight line, because the magnetic force has no effect
A parabola, similar to projectile motion
An ellipse that gradually spirals outward
questions.correct_answer: A circle, because the magnetic force always acts perpendicular to the velocity
questions.explanation: Since the magnetic force is always perpendicular to velocity, it changes only the direction of motion, not the speed, producing uniform circular motion.

questions.question: The force on a straight current-carrying conductor of length L carrying current I, placed in a uniform magnetic field B, is given by:
options: F = BIL sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the conductor and the field
questions.correct_answer: F = BIL sin(theta), where theta is the angle between the conductor and the field
questions.explanation: The force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is F = BIL sin(theta), reaching a maximum of BIL when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and zero when parallel to it.

questions.question: A straight conductor of length 0.5 m carrying a current of 4 A is placed perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of flux density 0.2 T. The force experienced by the conductor is:
questions.explanation: F = BIL = 0.2 x 4 x 0.5 = 0.4 N, since the conductor is perpendicular to the field (sin90 = 1).

questions.question: The direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field can be predicted using:
questions.correct_answer: Fleming's left-hand rule
questions.explanation: Fleming's left-hand rule (motor rule) relates the directions of the field, current, and resulting force/motion for a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

questions.question: A rectangular current loop placed in a uniform magnetic field experiences a torque that:
options: Tends to rotate the loop so its magnetic moment aligns with the field
Always pushes the loop out of the field entirely
Is zero regardless of the loop's orientation
Only acts when the loop carries no current
questions.correct_answer: Tends to rotate the loop so its magnetic moment aligns with the field
questions.explanation: The torque on a current loop in a magnetic field is tau = m x B (m being the magnetic moment), which acts to rotate the loop toward alignment of its moment with B, the principle behind electric motors and galvanometers.

questions.question: The torque on a planar current loop of area A, carrying current I, with N turns, in a uniform magnetic field B, when the plane of the loop makes an angle theta with the field, is given by:
questions.correct_answer: tau = NBIA sin(theta)
questions.explanation: Torque on a current loop is tau = NBIA sin(theta), where theta is measured between the field and the plane of the coil (equivalently, between the normal to the coil and the field gives a cosine form -- the sine form used here follows the standard convention with theta between B and the coil plane).

questions.question: Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction states that the induced EMF in a circuit is:
options: Proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit
Proportional to the magnetic flux itself, regardless of how it changes
Independent of any change in magnetic flux
Proportional to the resistance of the circuit only
questions.correct_answer: Proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linked with the circuit
questions.explanation: Faraday's law states EMF = -N(dPhi/dt), so induction requires a changing flux; a constant flux, however large, induces no EMF.

questions.question: Lenz's law states that the direction of an induced current is such that:
options: It opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
It always reinforces the change in magnetic flux that produced it
It flows in the same direction as the applied EMF always
questions.correct_answer: It opposes the change in magnetic flux that produced it
questions.explanation: Lenz's law is a consequence of energy conservation: the induced current creates its own magnetic field that opposes the change in the original flux, requiring work to be done against this opposition.

questions.question: A bar magnet is pushed into a coil of wire connected to a galvanometer. As the magnet moves further into the coil, the induced current, by Lenz's law, flows in a direction that makes the coil's near face:
options: Have no magnetic polarity at all
questions.correct_answer: Repel the approaching magnet
questions.explanation: By Lenz's law, the induced current opposes the increasing flux caused by the approaching magnet, so the coil's near face develops a pole that repels the magnet, resisting its motion.

questions.question: Motional EMF is induced in a straight conducting rod of length L moving with velocity v perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field B, and is given by:
questions.correct_answer: EMF = BLv
questions.explanation: As the rod moves through the field, the magnetic force on its free charges separates them, building up an EMF given by EMF = BLv (for B, L, and v mutually perpendicular).

questions.question: A conducting rod of length 0.8 m moves with a velocity of 5 m/s perpendicular to a magnetic field of flux density 0.4 T, with the field, rod, and velocity all mutually perpendicular. The motional EMF induced is:
Self-inductance of a coil is defined as the property by which:
options: A changing current in the coil induces an EMF in the same coil, opposing the change
A steady current in the coil produces a constant magnetic field only
Two separate coils exchange energy through a shared magnetic flux
The coil's resistance changes with current
questions.correct_answer: A changing current in the coil induces an EMF in the same coil, opposing the change
questions.explanation: Self-inductance L relates the induced EMF in a coil to the rate of change of its own current: EMF = -L(dI/dt), the induced EMF always opposing the change (Lenz's law).

questions.question: The unit of inductance, the henry, is defined such that one henry corresponds to:
options: An induced EMF of one volt when the current changes at a rate of one ampere per second
A current of one ampere flowing through a resistance of one ohm
A magnetic flux of one weber linking one turn
An EMF of one volt maintained for one second
questions.correct_answer: An induced EMF of one volt when the current changes at a rate of one ampere per second
questions.explanation: By definition, EMF = -L(dI/dt), so L = 1 henry when a rate of change of current of 1 A/s produces an induced EMF of 1 V.

questions.question: Mutual inductance between two coils describes:
options: The EMF induced in one coil due to a changing current in a neighbouring coil
The resistance shared between two coils connected in series
The self-inductance of a single isolated coil
The capacitance formed between two nearby coils
questions.correct_answer: The EMF induced in one coil due to a changing current in a neighbouring coil
questions.explanation: Mutual inductance M links the changing current in one coil to the EMF induced in a second, magnetically coupled coil: EMF2 = -M(dI1/dt).

questions.question: The energy stored in the magnetic field of an inductor L carrying current I is given by:
questions.explanation: Analogous to the energy stored in a capacitor, the energy stored in an inductor's magnetic field is U = (1/2)LI^2.

questions.question: For an alternating current (AC) that varies sinusoidally, the root-mean-square (RMS) value of the current is related to its peak (maximum) value I0 by:
questions.correct_answer: I(rms) = I0 / sqrt(2)
questions.explanation: For a sinusoidal waveform, the RMS value equals the peak value divided by the square root of 2, which is the value that would deliver the same average power as a DC current of that magnitude.

questions.question: The RMS value of an alternating current is significant because it represents:
options: The equivalent steady (DC) current that would produce the same average heating (power dissipation) effect in a resistor
The maximum instantaneous value the current ever reaches
The average value of the current over one full cycle, which is otherwise zero
The frequency of the alternating current
questions.correct_answer: The equivalent steady (DC) current that would produce the same average heating (power dissipation) effect in a resistor
questions.explanation: Since the true average of a symmetric sinusoid is zero, RMS is used instead because it corresponds to the DC current giving the same average power dissipation in a resistive load.

questions.question: An AC supply has a peak voltage of 311 V (typical of 220 V mains). The RMS voltage is approximately:
questions.explanation: V(rms) = V0/sqrt(2) = 311/1.414 is approximately 220 V, which is the standard quoted mains voltage.

questions.question: Capacitive reactance, the opposition offered by a capacitor to alternating current, is given by:
questions.correct_answer: X_C = 1/(2 pi f C)
questions.explanation: Capacitive reactance is inversely proportional to both frequency and capacitance: X_C = 1/(omega C) = 1/(2 pi f C).

questions.question: Inductive reactance, the opposition offered by an inductor to alternating current, is given by:
questions.correct_answer: X_L = 2 pi f L
questions.explanation: Inductive reactance is directly proportional to both frequency and inductance: X_L = omega L = 2 pi f L.

questions.question: As the frequency of an AC supply increases, the capacitive reactance of a capacitor:
questions.correct_answer: Decreases
questions.explanation: Since X_C = 1/(2 pi f C), reactance is inversely proportional to frequency, so it decreases as frequency rises.

questions.question: As the frequency of an AC supply increases, the inductive reactance of an inductor:
questions.correct_answer: Increases
questions.explanation: Since X_L = 2 pi f L, reactance is directly proportional to frequency, so it increases as frequency rises.

questions.question: In a series RLC circuit driven by an AC source, the total opposition to current flow, called impedance Z, is given by:
options: Z = R x X_L x X_C
questions.correct_answer: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2)
questions.explanation: Because resistance and reactance are out of phase, impedance in a series RLC circuit combines them as the hypotenuse of a right triangle: Z = sqrt(R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2).

questions.question: In a series RLC circuit, resonance occurs at the frequency where:
options: The inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C)
The capacitance equals the inductance numerically
The impedance is at its maximum value
questions.correct_answer: The inductive reactance equals the capacitive reactance (X_L = X_C)
questions.explanation: At resonance, X_L and X_C cancel exactly, leaving impedance at its minimum value (equal to R), which maximizes the current for a given applied voltage.

questions.question: The resonant frequency of a series RLC circuit is given by:
questions.correct_answer: f0 = 1 / (2 pi sqrt(LC))
questions.explanation: Setting X_L = X_C and solving for f gives the resonant frequency formula f0 = 1/(2 pi sqrt(LC)).

questions.question: At resonance in a series RLC circuit, the impedance of the circuit is:
options: At its minimum, equal to the resistance R alone
At its maximum, equal to R + X_L + X_C
questions.correct_answer: At its minimum, equal to the resistance R alone
questions.explanation: Since X_L and X_C cancel at resonance, Z = sqrt(R^2 + 0^2) = R, the minimum possible impedance for the circuit.

questions.question: The power factor of an AC circuit is defined as:
options: The cosine of the phase angle between the current and the applied voltage
The ratio of peak voltage to peak current
The ratio of resistance to reactance
The sine of the phase angle between voltage and current
questions.correct_answer: The cosine of the phase angle between the current and the applied voltage
questions.explanation: Power factor = cos(phi), where phi is the phase difference between voltage and current; it indicates what fraction of the apparent power (VI) is actually real (average) power delivered.

questions.question: For a purely resistive AC circuit (no reactance), the power factor is:
options: 1 (unity), because voltage and current are in phase
0, because voltage and current are 90 degrees out of phase
questions.correct_answer: 1 (unity), because voltage and current are in phase
questions.explanation: In a purely resistive circuit, current and voltage rise and fall together (zero phase difference), so cos(0) = 1, the maximum possible power factor.

questions.question: For a purely inductive or purely capacitive AC circuit (no resistance), the power factor is:
options: 0, because voltage and current are 90 degrees out of phase
1, because they are perfectly in phase
questions.correct_answer: 0, because voltage and current are 90 degrees out of phase
questions.explanation: In a purely reactive circuit, current and voltage are 90 degrees out of phase, giving cos(90) = 0, meaning no net (average) power is actually delivered even though current flows.

questions.question: The average (real) power delivered to an AC circuit is given by:
questions.correct_answer: P = V(rms) I(rms) cos(phi)
questions.explanation: Real power accounts for the phase difference between voltage and current using the power factor cos(phi); V(rms)I(rms) alone gives the apparent power.

questions.question: Diamagnetic materials, when placed in an external magnetic field, become:
options: Weakly magnetized in a direction opposite to the applied field
Strongly magnetized in the same direction as the applied field
Permanently magnetized even after the field is removed
Completely unaffected by any magnetic field
questions.correct_answer: Weakly magnetized in a direction opposite to the applied field
questions.explanation: Diamagnetic materials (e.g., bismuth, copper) acquire a weak induced magnetization opposing the applied field, resulting in a small negative magnetic susceptibility.

questions.question: Paramagnetic materials, when placed in an external magnetic field, become:
options: Weakly magnetized in the same direction as the applied field
Weakly magnetized in a direction opposite to the applied field
questions.correct_answer: Weakly magnetized in the same direction as the applied field
questions.explanation: Paramagnetic materials (e.g., aluminium, platinum) have unpaired electrons whose magnetic moments partially align with the applied field, giving a small positive susceptibility, but this magnetization disappears once the field is removed.

questions.question: Ferromagnetic materials, such as iron, cobalt, and nickel, are characterized by:
options: Strong magnetization that can persist even after the external field is removed, due to aligned magnetic domains
Weak magnetization that always opposes the applied field
No response whatsoever to external magnetic fields
Magnetization only possible at extremely high temperatures
questions.correct_answer: Strong magnetization that can persist even after the external field is removed, due to aligned magnetic domains
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials contain domains of aligned atomic magnetic moments that can be strongly reinforced by an external field and can retain a net magnetization (remanence) after the field is removed.

questions.question: The temperature above which a ferromagnetic material loses its ferromagnetic properties and becomes paramagnetic is called:
questions.correct_answer: The Curie temperature
questions.explanation: Above the Curie temperature, thermal agitation overcomes the alignment of magnetic domains, and the material's ordered ferromagnetism breaks down into disordered paramagnetic behaviour.

questions.question: A step-up transformer is used to:
options: Increase the AC voltage while decreasing the current, based on electromagnetic induction between coils
Increase both voltage and current simultaneously
Store electrical energy in a magnetic field permanently
questions.correct_answer: Increase the AC voltage while decreasing the current, based on electromagnetic induction between coils
questions.explanation: A transformer uses mutual inductance between a primary and secondary coil; a step-up transformer has more secondary turns than primary turns, raising voltage while lowering current to conserve power (ideally).

questions.question: Two long, straight, parallel wires carrying current in the same direction will:
questions.correct_answer: Attract each other
questions.explanation: Each wire's magnetic field exerts a force on the other's current-carrying charges; when the currents flow in the same direction, this results in a net attractive force between the wires.

questions.question: A galvanometer's high sensitivity to small currents, exploited in devices like the moving-coil galvanometer, arises fundamentally from the principle that:
options: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque proportional to the current, causing it to deflect
The coil heats up and expands when current flows
The coil's resistance decreases sharply with current
Static electric charge builds up on the coil
questions.correct_answer: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field experiences a torque proportional to the current, causing it to deflect
questions.explanation: The moving-coil galvanometer relies directly on the torque tau = NBIA sin(theta) experienced by a current loop in a magnetic field, which is balanced against a restoring spring to give a deflection proportional to current.
